title: Lord of the Flies: A Harmful Distortion of Children's Nature
author: Peter Gray
summary: Peter Gray argues that William Golding's Lord of the Flies has done lasting damage by entrenching the myth that children left unsupervised will devolve into violence and savagery. He counters with a real case recovered by historian Rutger Bregman: a group of Tongan schoolboys stranded on an uninhabited island for 15 months who cooperated throughout, resolved quarrels peacefully, kept fire alive, tended a garden, cared for an injured companion, and built a guitar from salvaged materials. Gray connects the novel's widespread assignment in schools to the foundational ideology of compulsory schooling—the assumption that children require adult authority to function—and notes that teachers who maintain classroom control are professionally rewarded regardless of whether they help children learn. He examines Golding's biography, noting the author acknowledged personal darkness (alcohol, violence, depression) and an admission of attempted rape at 18, and argues his novel reflects one man's struggle with his own demons rather than universal children's nature. Gray's conclusion is that authoritarian control more often incites than prevents children's brutality, and the Golding narrative deserves critical interrogation rather than treated as natural truth. The article closes with an invitation to readers to share whether their experience with actual children confirms or disconfirms Golding's premise.
points: The real-world Tongan castaway case—six schoolboys stranded 15 months under conditions mirroring the novel—produced cooperation, mutual care, and maintained fire rather than violence, directly falsifying Golding's premise.

Lord of the Flies is widely assigned in schools precisely because it supports the foundational assumption of compulsory schooling: that children without adult supervision produce chaos—making it an ideological tool rather than a neutral literary text.

Golding's biographer documents that the author's worldview was shaped by his acknowledged personal struggle with darkness, not by observation of children; the novel reflects one man's psyche projected onto the species.
When real children face genuine danger, their documented behavioral response is cooperative survival—as in the Lost Boys of Sudan and the Tongan castaways—not the violence Golding depicts.

Authoritarian control more often incites children's brutality than prevents it; the chaotic violence Golding depicts is a projection of classroom anxiety, not evidence about what children do when genuinely free.
quotes: 'Lord of the Flies' is the shorthand that people use to express the belief that children are incapable of self-discipline and will eventually run amok and attack one another if not supervised by adults. My first response, when I hear this expression, has always been, 'Well, you know, Lord of the Flies is a work of fiction.'

In the real world, children rarely, if ever, act like the fictitious children of Lord of the Flies. When children become brutal, there are usually adults leading or provoking the brutality. When real children are abandoned and realize their lives are in danger, their survival instincts kick in and lead them to cooperate even more than they normally do.

The boys did quarrel, but they developed ways of resolving their quarrels peacefully. One of them managed to create a fire by rubbing sticks together, and they carefully kept the fire going the whole time they were there.

I think it's no surprise that this book is so often assigned in school. It's a morality tale that fits with a fundamental assumption behind compulsory schooling—the assumption that kids just make a mess of things if left to their own devices.

Golding himself had a very dark side, with which he struggled throughout his life. In a memoir that he never published, Golding admitted to attempting to rape a 15-year-old girl when he, at age 18, was home from college. He drank heavily throughout his adult life, sometimes behaved violently when drunk, was often depressed and had a turbulent relationship with his own children and wife.
Authoritarian control much more often incites violence than prevents it.
